strengths: Explores an interesting and underexplored direction: using a purely autoregressive transformer framework over vector-quantized 3D Gaussian representations for 3D scene generation, presenting a viable alternative to prevailing diffusion- and flow-matching-based methods.

Well-motivated technical designs, including interleaving position and feature tokens with decoupled vocabularies and projection heads, using Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ), and employing 4D Rotary Positional Embeddings (3D spatial coordinates + token type) to alleviate serialization artifacts.

Demonstrates versatile capabilities within a single model architecture, including unconditional synthesis, prefix-conditioned completion/inpainting, and sliding-window outpainting for large-scale environments (e.g., 12 m × 12 m scenes).

Strong quantitative results on the PhotoShape chair benchmark, where GaussianGPT achieves competitive geometric fidelity (MMD) and outperforms strong baselines like L3DG and DiffRF in FID, KID, and COV.
Clear writing and thorough documentation of training hyperparameters, sampling mechanisms, and preliminary real-world results on ScanNet++ in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Evaluation on indoor scenes (3D-FRONT and ASE) is almost entirely qualitative. Quantitative metrics on scene generation (e.g., rendered FID/KID, layout validity, or physical plausibility metrics compared against L3DG or other scene synthesis baselines) are missing.

Ablation studies are limited in scope. While the comparison of serialization orders (Tab. 2) is informative, other crucial design components—such as the impact of 3D RoPE versus standard 1D RoPE, LFQ versus standard VQ-VAE, and separated versus shared token vocabularies—are not quantitatively evaluated.

Inference latency is high for scene synthesis. As reported in Appendix B, generating a 12 m × 12 m scene requires ~6,000 seconds on a high-end GH200 GPU (~90 seconds per 4 m × 4 m chunk), which presents practical scalability challenges compared to fast feed-forward or accelerated diffusion approaches.

Reconstruction resolution and fidelity in full scenes are constrained by the 20 cm latent voxel grid, leading to smoothed geometry, loss of fine object parts, and visible artifacts, especially in real-world ScanNet++ experiments.

strengths: Conceptual formulation: Exploring an autoregressive, next-token prediction paradigm for 3D Gaussian Splatting provides an interesting and complementary alternative to the prevailing diffusion and flow-matching approaches.

Well-motivated architectural adaptations: The decoupling of geometry and appearance via interleaved position and feature tokens, combined with 4D RoPE (incorporating 3D coordinate offsets and a token-type indicator), sensibly addresses the loss of spatial locality inherent to 1D serialization.

Versatility of applications: The causal autoregressive formulation naturally accommodates scene completion, prefix conditioning, and arbitrary sliding-window outpainting within a single model architecture without requiring dedicated inpainting networks or specialized diffusion guidance.

Strong shape synthesis results: On the PhotoShape benchmark (Table 1), the method outperforms existing methods including L3DG and DiffRF across FID, KID, and COV metrics, showing that discrete tokenization of Gaussians can be competitive with continuous diffusion models.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation for scene-level generation: While the paper is framed around 3D Gaussian scene generation, quantitative metrics (e.g., FID, KID, CLIP score, coverage, or geometric realism metrics) are exclusively reported for single-object chair synthesis (Table 1). The scene-level evaluation on ASE and 3D-FRONT is strictly qualitative.

Limited baseline comparisons on scenes: Scene generation is compared only qualitatively against a single baseline (L3DG). Comparisons against other established 3D scene generative approaches (e.g., DiffuScene, SceneFormer, ATISS) or user studies assessing layout realism and visual quality are missing.

Inference latency and reliance on resampling heuristics: Autoregressive generation over thousands of tokens is computationally heavy, taking approximately 90 seconds for a 4m x 4m chunk and ~6,000 seconds (~1.6 hours) on an enterprise GH200 GPU for a 12m x 12m scene. Furthermore, generating coherent scenes requires an ad-hoc heuristic of repeatedly resampling empty columns up to five times to prevent collapse into empty space.

Visual fidelity and boundary coherence in scene synthesis: Qualitative results (Figures 4, 9, 10) show relatively coarse object geometry, noticeable blurriness, and repetitive object placements, indicating that the sparse latent grid resolution (20 cm voxel size) struggles to preserve fine structural and textural details in complex rooms.

strengths: Novel and timely exploration: While most contemporary 3D Gaussian generative models rely on diffusion or flow-matching formulations, this work presents a compelling, fully autoregressive transformer pipeline for structured 3D Gaussian scene generation and completion.

Well-motivated technical design: The serialization of sparse 3D latent grids into alternating position and feature tokens with decoupled vocabularies, combined with a 4D rotary positional embedding (3D RoPE + token type), elegantly mitigates the spatial locality loss inherent to 1D sequence flattening.

Inherent versatility of the autoregressive formulation: The method handles unconditional generation, structured completion (inpainting via prefix prompting), and infinite outpainting via a sliding window within a single model architecture without task-specific modifications.

Strong quantitative performance on object benchmarks: On the PhotoShape chair generation benchmark (Table 1), GaussianGPT achieves state-of-the-art results, outperforming diffusion-based L3DG and DiffRF across FID (5.68 vs. 8.49), KID, and Coverage.

Insightful ablations: The comparison between xyz ordering and space-filling curves (Hilbert, Z-order) in Table 2 provides valuable empirical evidence that simple rasterization suffices when coordinate-aware 3D RoPE is employed.
weaknesses: Lack of quantitative evaluation on scene generation: Despite the paper's primary focus and title centering on full 3D scene generation, quantitative metrics (e.g., rendering FID/KID, geometric fidelity, scene layout plausibility) are only reported for object-level synthesis (PhotoShape). The scene-level evaluation on 3D-FRONT and ASE is purely qualitative.

High inference latency: As reported in Appendix B, generating a 12 m × 12 m scene requires approximately 6,000 seconds (~100 minutes) on a high-end GH200 GPU, and even a single 4 m × 4 m chunk takes around 90 seconds. Autoregressive sampling speed is a major practical bottleneck compared to accelerated diffusion solvers, which warrants prominent discussion and comparison in the main text.

Coarse spatial resolution and appearance fidelity: Operating at a latent voxel resolution of 20 cm for scenes leads to noticeable geometric oversmoothing and loss of fine-grained structures in scene renders. Additionally, view-dependent effects (spherical harmonics) are omitted for scenes, restricting visual realism.

Reliance on sampling heuristics: The large-scale outpainting procedure relies on rejection sampling (resampling up to five times when predicted columns are empty) to prevent degenerating into empty space, indicating that unconditional likelihood modeling over sparse chunks can struggle with empty-space bias.

strengths: Presents a novel and sound formulation for 3D Gaussian generation by framing it as a purely autoregressive next-token prediction problem, offering a compelling alternative to dominant diffusion-based approaches.

Well-motivated architectural designs tailored to 3D representation: interleaved position and feature tokens with decoupled vocabularies, and a 4D RoPE mechanism (3D spatial offsets + token type) that effectively removes sensitivity to serialization ordering.

Inherent versatility of the causal transformer formulation is well exploited, enabling seamless unconditional generation, scene completion from arbitrary prefixes without retrained conditioning heads, and open-ended scene outpainting.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across object-level (PhotoShape) and scene-level (3D-FRONT, ASE, ScanNet++ v2) benchmarks, supported by meaningful ablations on serialization curves and core positional encoding components.
Thorough and transparent analysis of limitations, including runtime benchmarks (Table 5) and error accumulation across large scene generation (Figure 9).
weaknesses: Sampling speed and computational overhead: Autoregressive token-by-token generation is substantially slower than diffusion baselines for unconditional chunk synthesis (78.1s vs 23.8s), and generating an extended 12m x 12m scene requires ~6,000s.

Mode coverage and geometry trade-off: In unconditional scene generation (Table 2), GaussianGPT exhibits noticeably lower coverage (COV: 0.548 vs 0.692) and higher MMD than L3DG, pointing to potential mode-collapse or conservative sampling in unconstrained settings.

Accumulation of errors during extended outpainting: Despite the proposed column resampling strategy, spatial degradation remains evident as the generation horizon expands away from the conditioning seed (as demonstrated in Fig. 9).
Currently restricted to unconditional generation and prefix completion, lacking semantic or multimodal control (e.g., text-guided or layout-guided scene synthesis).

strengths: Novel and timely formulation: While current 3D Gaussian scene generation methods almost exclusively rely on diffusion or flow-matching formulations, this work presents a compelling, fully autoregressive alternative (GaussianGPT) that frames 3D scene generation as next-token prediction over vector-quantized spatial latents.

Well-engineered representation and architecture: The proposed design effectively addresses key hurdles in sequential 3D modeling by interleaving position and feature tokens with separate vocabularies, adopting Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) for dense codebook utilization, and introducing 4D RoPE (3D spatial coordinates + token type) to preserve spatial locality irrespective of serialization order.

Versatile and unified generative capabilities: Benefiting from the causal autoregressive structure, the model handles unconditional synthesis, arbitrary scene completion/inpainting via prefix prompting, and large-scale scene extension via sliding-window outpainting within a single model without requiring specialized architectural adapters.

Thorough experimental validation and ablation studies: The paper validates the approach across object (PhotoShape) and scene datasets (3D-FRONT, ASE, and ScanNet++ v2 in the appendix). The empirical analysis is well-controlled, comparing against competitive baselines like L3DG under identical chunked settings, and provides insightful ablations on serialization traversal orders, PE strategies, and quantization parameters.
weaknesses: Inference speed and computational overhead: Due to sequential token sampling over long contexts (up to 16k tokens), unconditional chunk generation is significantly slower than diffusion baselines (78.1s vs. 23.8s on an A100 GPU), and synthesizing a 12m x 12m scene takes roughly 6,000s on a GH200. Although techniques like speculative decoding and decode kernels are discussed as future work, inference latency remains a notable practical drawback.

Error accumulation and drift in long-horizon outpainting: As demonstrated in Fig. 9 and Sec. C, generative quality noticeably degrades as generation progresses further from the seed context along the serialization axis. The generation relies on heuristic backtracking/resampling to avoid drifting into empty or out-of-distribution space.

Autoencoder compression bottleneck: To make sequence lengths manageable for the causal transformer context window, the model requires 3x downsampling (yielding 20cm latent voxels). This aggressive compression causes a drop in reconstruction fidelity (e.g., PSNR around 25 dB) and restricts the representation of fine-grained geometry and thin structures, which becomes especially visible in the real-world ScanNet++ experiments.

Lack of semantic or multimodal conditioning: The framework is demonstrated primarily on unconditional generation, outpainting, and spatial completion. Extending the model to support text-to-scene or multi-view image prompts would significantly improve practical utility and enable direct comparison with modern multimodal 3D generative frameworks.

strengths: Explores a timely and underexplored direction: applying autoregressive sequence modeling (next-token prediction) to 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representations, offering an alternative paradigm to dominant diffusion and flow-matching approaches.

Well-motivated architecture design: using sparse 3D convolutional autoencoding with Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ), decoupling geometry and appearance via interleaved position/feature tokens with separate heads, and incorporating a 4D RoPE (3D spatial coordinates + token-type indicator) to mitigate sequence linearization biases.

Natural unified support for unconditional generation, scene completion via prefix conditioning, and arbitrary outpainting without requiring specialized conditioning adapters or reverse diffusion heuristics (e.g., RePaint).

Thorough empirical investigation and ablation studies, covering serialization strategies (xyz vs. Z-order vs. Hilbert), vocabulary designs, positional embeddings, codebook configurations, and inference efficiency/memory trade-offs.
weaknesses: Coarse visual and geometric fidelity: Due to the need to keep sequence lengths manageable for the causal transformer, the 3D autoencoder downsamples to a coarse 20 cm latent grid. As seen in the qualitative figures, generated indoor scenes exhibit noticeable blurriness, simple geometries, and lack the fine structural and textural details achieved by state-of-the-art scene synthesis pipelines.

Lower diversity in unconditional generation: As reported in Table 2, GaussianGPT suffers from substantially lower coverage (COV of 0.548 vs. 0.692 for L3DG) and worse MMD in unconditional scene generation, reflecting the well-known tendency of autoregressive models to suffer from mode collapse/reduced distribution coverage compared to diffusion baselines.

Inference latency and error accumulation: Autoregressive sampling is slow (78 s per chunk on an A100 vs. 24 s for L3DG; ~6,000 s for a 12m x 12m scene on a GH200). Furthermore, large-scale outpainting suffers from clear spatial drift and error accumulation across chunk frontiers (as documented in Figure 9), requiring ad-hoc resampling heuristics to prevent empty or degraded predictions.

Limited real-world applicability: The model relies heavily on axis-aligned synthetic indoor datasets (3D-FRONT, ASE). As demonstrated in Appendix A, performance degrades markedly when fine-tuned on real-world scans (ScanNet++), where sensor noise, unobserved regions, and arbitrary orientations pose significant hurdles for the current tokenization scheme.
